cells.tense: You're standing here with the fire lit and your hands free to carry it.
cells.ask: Hand one thing you've been carrying to its own momentum, then give an hour to the thing that actually wants you.
cells.core:
You light fires people want to stand near, and right now you can put something down without losing it. The confidence shows up in small exchanges — someone leans in, the room warms, the next right move turns up on its own. You're not performing it and not chasing it. It's just operating, and its worth is that it's offered rather than forced.

The squeeze comes when a stretch like this gets read as proof to grip harder. That's where the light turns into load. The practice is keeping the letting-go as clean as it's been, so the fire travels where it's actually wanted instead of where you're still pushing.
cells.sheetLine: You let go, and what's left is worth carrying.
cells.verb: Lighting the fire in others before the direction is fully known
cells.place: Where what you've held is set down to make room

cells.tense: You're already living in the moment after the release lands, before it's started.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding and put it down for a day without telling anyone you did.
cells.core:
You're burning ahead of where the fire actually is. Someone should have caught the spark by now, the next step should already be lit — and you're pushing at a future that hasn't arrived. The energy is real, but it's running on force instead of on what you've actually grown. You can tell because the thing you're still holding has started to feel like weight.

This is the same fire leaning forward so hard it tips. More fuel won't help. The moment you're actually in is where what you made is finished enough to stand. The spark lands when it comes out of what's already complete, not out of what you're still pushing toward. Ease up on the future and the present catches up.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing at a future that hasn't arrived yet.

cells.tense: You let go of something real and then stayed outside the next thing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're still holding that's finished, set it down visibly, and give ten minutes to something small you'd tend for no reason.
cells.core:
The fire is still there — you can feel it when someone else's excitement brushes against yours — but you've stopped lighting anything of your own. What you released is behind you, and what should have taken its place hasn't been picked up. The spark didn't go out. It just isn't being offered anywhere.

This isn't a courage problem. It's a tending one. You've been waiting for the spark to arrive on its own instead of giving one small thing your daily attention. The fire you miss isn't found, it's grown — badly at first, then steadier — and the waiting is what's keeping it out of reach.
cells.sheetLine: You let the fire go and then waited for it to return.

cells.tense: The grip is loose in your hands and you're calling it the situation letting go.
cells.ask: Say out loud, to whoever's around, that you're the one who chose to put that down.
cells.core:
The heat comes off your own hands — you start something, someone catches it, and it travels without you running after it. That's the fire doing what it does when you're not clutching it, and people near you feel it as ease. Nothing is chasing you and nothing is being pushed. The spark is simply doing its work in the open air.

What's happening instead is quieter. Something loosened — you stopped steering, you didn't argue this time, you left the room on its own — and you're filing that under things working out. But you took the pressure off. That part is yours, and it's going unnamed. The next release is easier when you know whose hand let it go.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one who let it go. Say so.
